Subject: Performance SLOs & Autoscaling - follow-up and next steps

Thanks again for the call this morning, Jordan — great to hear more about Acme's real-time summarization use case. Quick recap and proposed next steps on the performance side so we can line this up with pricing and a Dedicated capacity proposal.

Recap / what you told us:
- Target tail latency (p95/p99) for live summarization: 200ms / 450ms for single-request streaming responses.
- Expected steady-state throughput: ~80 reqs/min, with ~150 reqs/min expected during peak/marketing events.
- Typical prompt lengths: 1.5k tokens; average response length: 250 tokens.
- Concurrency goal: 40 concurrent streams during peaks.

Open questions we flagged on the call:
1) Burst tolerance: how long are peak bursts (minutes vs hours)?
2) Acceptable degradation model: queueing vs graceful quality/fallback model?
3) Any regulatory constraints requiring warm-pool-only solutions?

Proposed next steps:
- We’ll run a short benchmark using your sample traces (you mentioned sending a CSV) to validate model footprint and expected CPU/GPU concurrency.
- Vivek will propose autoscaling targets (scale-up times, warm pool size, queueing behavior) mapped to the p95/p99 SLO.
- Send over any additional traces and the list of models you plan to evaluate (model id + quantization if known).

If that looks right I’ll schedule a 30-min follow-up with Vivek and Dylan to review the benchmark results and a draft autoscaling SLA.

Thanks,

Marissa Cole
Account Executive, Redwood Inference

Thanks Marissa — correct summary. A couple clarifications from our side:

- Burst profile: mostly short spikes at start of hour and during product announcements. Typical burst window is 5-12 minutes; rare sustained events ~45-60 minutes (once per month).
- Degradation model: we prefer queueing for short bursts (so we preserve p95 target) and then fall back to a smaller, cheaper model variant when queue depth exceeds threshold. We do not want hard failures for customer-facing flows.
- Warm pools: we can tolerate a small warm pool for ~10% of peak concurrency but would like to avoid a large always-on pool due to cost.

Can you confirm expected scale-up time for a cold-to-warm node and how quickly Redwood can spin up additional workers to reach 2x baseline concurrency? Also attaching a sample trace now.

Jordan

Jordan — great, thanks for the trace. Vivek and I dug in with the runtime team and here's a pragmatic mapping from your SLOs to autoscaling/operational behavior. High-level first, then suggested config.

High-level:
- Cold start to first warm worker: ~60-90s for large models (2–4x faster for quantized variants). Cold startup includes kernel/cuda context init + model load.
- Warm-pool spin-up (pre-warmed VM/container with model loaded, ready to accept work): ~6–12s to transition to active for additional workers on the same host.
- Autoscaling policy: We recommend a hybrid approach — small warm pool sized at 8–10% of your target peak concurrency plus rapid scaling with pre-warmed instances for predictable bursts.
- Queueing: Short bursts (<=12 minutes): queueing target of 250ms max queuing latency keeps p95 under 200ms for your workload based on the sample trace. For sustained events (>20 minutes) we recommend fallback to a smaller model variant after queue depth threshold (~60 concurrent queued requests).

Suggested config (starting point):
- Baseline dedicated capacity to sustain 80 reqs/min with 40 concurrent streaming sessions (this maps to 1x pool of N GPUs depending on model).
- Warm pool: 4 pre-warmed workers (models loaded, idle) — approx 10% of expected peak; expected to absorb immediate bursts and cut tail latency.
- Scale policy: add 4 workers per scale-up step (each step adds ~6–12s active capacity if on pre-warmed hosts, 60–90s if on cold hosts). Aim to reach 2x baseline in ~2 scale steps under pre-warmed conditions (~12–24s effective ramp).
- Fallback model: automatic routing to a smaller quantized variant if queue depth > 60 for >30s. Logging + alerting on every fallback event.

Attachments: I’ve attached our autoscaling playbook and a quick CSV with baseline latency projections from your sample trace. These include the internal assumptions (tokenization, median generation token time) that we used.

Next steps / proposal:
- Technical review: let Vivek and Dylan pull in one of our runtime engineers for a 30-min run-through of the playbook and get your signoff on the baseline config.
- Benchmark run: we’ll run the trace in our dedicated test harness and share a short report by EOD Wed.
- Pricing: Post-benchmark, I’ll follow up with a draft Dedicated capacity quote sized to the baseline + warm-pool config + burst allowance.

If that plan works I’ll set up the two follow-ups (technical + benchmark result review).

Best,

Marissa Cole
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
